selectionPolicy: Kaishi supplies candidate headwords, not an authoritative JLPT syllabus.
Resolve existing terms, readings, variants, meanings and compositional forms before adding any SRS unit.
Require clear everyday beginner usefulness and a specific primary beginner-material reference for each imported word.
Irodori through Elementary 2 is an approximate N4 ability benchmark, not an official word-by-word JLPT classification.
Use supplemental scope for these practical additions while retaining the existing exam-oriented core inventory.
All meanings, examples and translations are authored for ChakuChaku; Kaishi/Japan Foundation sentences, images and recordings are not imported.
New examples use existing N5 vocabulary around the target, with familiar basic grammar. New words share the normal N4 introduction budget.

irodori-n4-scope.title: Japan Foundation: Irodori and JLPT N4, FAQ 11–12

entries.reason: Expresses limited ability or a mild dislike in everyday conversations, including food preferences. It adds a common alternative to 好き, 嫌い, 上手 and 下手.
A basic compliment for people, clothes, places and gifts. Explicitly taught in Irodori beginner materials.
Describes an uninterrupted state or activity in routine accounts of a day. This initial gloss and example target the continuous-time sense, not every comparative or spatial use.
The existing N4 けがする card already teaches getting hurt, with けが explicitly present in its example. Do not create an additional noun SRS card solely to match Kaishi’s 怪我 headword.
The everyday expression 調子が悪い is explicitly taught in elementary health communication. The example identifies bodily condition rather than a musical sense.
Lets learners discuss confidence in language and practical abilities. It is a separate word from the homophone 地震; its new audio slug preserves the existing earthquake recording.
Useful for trust, beliefs and everyday interpersonal communication. Included in Irodori Elementary 2 even though the legacy JLPT source places it later.
Covers helping or rescuing someone in difficulty, extending beyond 手伝う for assisting with a task. Explicitly present in Irodori Elementary 2.
Basic home and workplace vocabulary for cleaning, room descriptions and problems with a building. Read ゆか, not the とこ in 床屋.
An elementary room-description and household-problem word explicitly taught with 床 in Irodori Elementary 2.

Needed for remaining food, drink, quantities and time. Its presence in Irodori Starter provides strong beginner-usefulness evidence; N4 is this app’s introduction choice for the current review batch. Keep the lexical noun 残り distinct from the existing verb 残る: the new example teaches noun + の for a remaining quantity.
Already taught at N4 with the required on-the-way/midway sense. Keep its existing SRS identity and examples; do not create a duplicate.
Primarily needed for fantasy and fictional settings; no clear everyday N4 task justifies prioritizing it in this batch.
A political/fantasy setting noun; lower priority than routine home, health and interpersonal communication for the current N4 goals.
A fiction and supernatural-content word; defer pending a separate need-based review rather than promoting it solely on media frequency.
A basic body part needed to describe pain to a doctor. Irodori teaches it in its elementary health lesson; the example targets the chest sense.
Needed to describe common shoulder pain and stiffness in elementary health communication. It is distinct from the existing homophone 方, whose recording is preserved.
A basic word for explaining lower-back pain, with a direct elementary health reference. The example makes the lower-back sense explicit.
Useful at a checkout and when carrying or packing purchases; explicitly taught in Irodori Starter. Existing 手袋 means gloves and does not teach this standalone word.
A basic location word for following directions inside a building, taught in Irodori Starter. Existing 奥さん, 置く and 億 are different words; a semantic audio slug preserves both existing おく recordings.
Lets learners discuss portions of food and other everyday quantities. Irodori Elementary 2 teaches it in a restaurant context.
Useful for discussing and recommending shops, places and entertainment. The example teaches the common 人気がある construction; Irodori has both the noun and that construction.
Expresses a lasting feeling of happiness and well-being, extending the existing words for being pleased or having fun. Explicitly taught as a na-adjective in Irodori Elementary 1.
Basic vocabulary for describing personal relationships, taught as boyfriend/girlfriend in Irodori Starter. The meaning specifies a romantic partner rather than a business partner.
Distinguishes an acquaintance from a friend, useful in introductions and everyday accounts of meeting people. Taught in the opening lesson of Irodori Elementary 1.
Useful for talking about trips and shared experiences. This lexical noun is explicitly taught in Irodori Elementary 1 and is distinct from the existing verb 思い出す, to remember.
Needed for simple hopes and future plans, explicitly taught in Irodori Elementary 2. This is not the existing 五日, five days/the fifth; it gets a separate recording and SRS identity.
A practical time expression for the current trip, attempt or occasion, distinct from 今, 前回 and 次回. Explicitly present in Irodori Elementary 2.
Useful for asking someone directly, arranging an in-person exchange and avoiding intermediaries. Explicitly taught in Irodori Elementary 2.
Needed for letters, parcels and deliveries. Irodori Elementary 2 explicitly teaches the delivery sense; it is an intransitive arrival, not sending or handing something over.
A useful verb for making social plans and inviting friends to activities. Explicitly taught in Irodori Elementary 2; the example uses the basic person を activity に pattern.
Useful for trying a dish, a product or a method. The lexical verb is explicitly taught in Irodori Elementary 1 and is distinct from the grammatical てみる construction.
A basic daily routine and workplace action, explicitly taught in Irodori Starter. Knowing the existing verb 着る alone does not independently teach this compound verb.
Useful when leaving luggage at a hotel or checking belongings at a facility. Irodori Elementary 2 teaches this safekeeping sense and its polite request form.

A practical verb for protection and following rules, both explicitly taught in Irodori beginner materials. The example teaches protection with familiar N5 vocabulary; it is not selected solely for fictional combat contexts.
